# Removing a Viscous Fan without the Serpentine Belt (1998 Land Rover Discovery)

The Power Assist Steering pump on your 1998 Land Rover Discovery failed spectacularly, shedding its pulley right beside the road. Getting to the replacement unit requires removing the viscous fan clutch, which involves undoing a left-hand-thread nut in the center of the coupling. The immediate problem is that you cannot stop the pulley from rotating because it sits on its own shaft rather than being bolted directly to the crankshaft.

Normally, this rotation issue is resolved by the serpentine belt; the tension holds the belt tight enough against the pulleys to act as a brake. However, with the PAS pulley missing, you cannot refit the belt. You are left with a spinning fan and a stubborn nut that refuses to budge.

The central bolt holding the viscous coupling spins freely because it is not keyed to the crankshaft but rather clamped onto a separate hub. Attempts to use the small bolts securing the pulley rim for extra purchase failed when two came undone, leaving only two remaining. Due to the hexagonal shape of the big nut, you cannot fit a ring spanner over the rim, and trying to use an open-ended wrench has already started rounding off the corners.

## The Physics of the Locknut

The viscous fan clutch on this model uses a specific locking mechanism. The large central nut is designed to be tightened against the viscous coupling housing while the entire assembly spins at high RPMs. Once cooled down, the torque drops significantly. To remove it safely, you need to create static friction between the tool and the rotating components without relying on an external belt tensioner.

Since a standard ring spanner cannot fit over the hex nut, and the pulley rim bolts are insufficient due to rounded edges, you must engage the shaft itself or find a way to clamp the assembly from the outside.

## Engaging the Shaft Directly

The most effective method involves bypassing the nut entirely and gripping the shaft that runs through the center of the viscous clutch. On many Land Rover Discovery models of this era, there is a specific splined section on the crankshaft or a dedicated locking tab designed for service removal.

If direct access to a locking tab is impossible due to the missing belt tensioner, you can fabricate a temporary wedge using a long bolt and a large washer. Thread a long bolt through the center of the viscous clutch assembly (using the existing hole in the big nut or finding a clearance hole near the hub). Place a substantial flat washer against the side of the viscous clutch housing that faces away from the engine block. This washer must be wider than the shaft but narrower than the coupling housing to avoid interference with adjacent components.

Once the bolt is threaded through, you can use a large socket or an impact wrench on the end of the bolt to clamp the assembly against the stationary part of the engine. The goal is to create enough friction so that when you turn the fan nut, the entire assembly stops spinning relative to the engine block.

## Using the Pulley Rim as a Brake

If engaging the shaft proves difficult due to space constraints, try utilizing the remaining two small bolts on the pulley rim more aggressively. Since you cannot fit a ring spanner, you can drill out the hexagonal heads of these remaining bolts and replace them with larger diameter bolts that allow for a box-end wrench or socket to engage fully.

Alternatively, if the pulley has any structural integrity left despite losing two bolts, you can attempt to wedge the rim itself. Place a piece of flat steel or a specialized fan clutch holder between the spinning pulley and the stationary engine block. Ensure the wedge is positioned where it will not damage the viscous coupling plates inside. The friction generated by this wedge should be sufficient to stop the rotation long enough to break the thread on the large nut.

## Thread Direction and Safety

Remember that the large central nut is left-hand-threaded. This means you must turn the tool counter-clockwise to loosen it, which is opposite to standard automotive fasteners. If your wrench setup creates too much resistance, the bolt may snap or the fan clutch may slip off, potentially causing injury or further damage to the viscous coupling internals.

If you manage to secure the assembly using one of the methods above, apply a penetrating oil like PB Blaster to the threads and let it sit for at least 15 minutes before attempting to loosen the nut. Apply steady pressure rather than jerking motions to avoid stripping the remaining bolt holes.

Once the nut is removed, inspect the viscous coupling plates. If they are worn or the clutch has failed catastrophically, replacing just the nut will not solve the overheating issue. The fan clutch must be replaced as a complete unit if the internal viscosity fluid has degraded or the plates are damaged.
